big_idea: Two small groups together make 5. Take some away — a smaller group is left.
learning_intention: We are learning all the ways to make 5 with two groups, and what is left when we take some away.
student_learning_goal: I can say all the ways to make 5 with two groups, and I can say what is left when I take some away.
success_criteria: I can build 5 using two cube colours in different ways.
I can say my number bond out loud: 'two and three make five.'
I can take cubes away and tell how many are left.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart 'Partners of 5' with 6 rows ready to fill: 0+5, 1+4, 2+3, 3+2, 4+1, 5+0
5 large foam cubes (red and yellow) for whole-group demos

OPTIONAL: Penny and Nick props from Lesson 1 — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 2 formative tracker (Partners of 5) — provided in assessment_suite stage
Sticky notes for child names beside each partner row

minds_on.hook: Penny has 5 snap-cubes for the snack shop — but they come in two colours. How many ways can she put them together?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Penny and 5 large foam cubes (3 red, 2 yellow).

'Friends — Penny is sorting cube-snacks for the Counting Shop. She has 5 cubes in all, but they come in TWO colours.' Snap the cubes together into one tower of 5: red-red-red-yellow-yellow. 'How many red? How many yellow? How many ALTOGETHER?' Take responses. Confirm: 'Three reds and two yellows make five altogether.' Write 3 + 2 = 5 on the anchor chart with the cube colours dotted beside.

Now break the tower apart and rebuild it differently: 1 red, 4 yellow. 'What if Penny made the train this way? How many of each colour? And how many altogether?' Children chorus: 'one and four make five.' Add 1 + 4 = 5 to the chart. 'These are PARTNERS of 5. Two parts that go together to make five. Today we are going to find ALL the partners of 5 — and then learn how to use them to take some away.'

Penny's refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'TWO PARTS make a WHOLE — that's how Penny adds!'
student_actions: Listen and watch Penny's cube tower being built and rebuilt.
Count the two colours and the total aloud as a class.
Read the partner-of-5 sentence aloud after the teacher writes it ('three and two make five').

action.activity_name: Partner Hunt — Building the Bonds of 5

steps.instruction: Whole group: each child gets 5 snap-cubes (mixed red and yellow). Teacher leads the class in building one tower of 5 together, then breaking it into TWO groups of any sizes. Children hold up their two pieces and call out their partner: 'I made two and three!'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Snap your five cubes together. Now break them into two pieces — any two pieces. Hold them up.' Walk through. 'Tell me your partners. I'll write them on our chart.' Each child reports; teacher tallies on the anchor chart with sticky notes.

steps.instruction: Class fills the Partners-of-5 chart together. Read every row aloud. Add the two missing rows (0+5 and 5+0) by asking 'is there a partner with NO yellow cubes?' and 'is there a partner with NO red cubes?'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Look at our chart. Did we get all six partners? Let me read what we have.' Read across: 0+5, 1+4, 2+3, 3+2, 4+1, 5+0. 'Six partners of five. Notice — when one part gets bigger, the other part gets smaller.'

steps.instruction: Introduce subtraction. Hold up a tower of 5. Say 'Penny had 5 cubes. Nick took 2 to make a customer's order. How many are LEFT?' Pull 2 cubes off the tower; show the 3 remaining. 'Five take away two leaves three.' Write 5 − 2 = 3 on the chart beside its partner 3 + 2 = 5.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Five take away two leaves three. Did we already KNOW three was a partner of two and five? Yes! Plus and minus are friends. If three and two make five, then five take away two leaves three.' Repeat with 1 and 4.

steps.instruction: Send pairs to their tables for the Partner Hunt game. Each pair has 5 cubes and a ten-frame mat (M4). Player A hides some cubes under their hand; Player B sees the rest and names the missing partner. Switch.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You and your partner are going to play the Partner Hunt. Player A — hide some of your cubes under your hand. Player B — look at what's showing. Tell your partner how many are HIDDEN. If three are showing, you say TWO are hiding. Then switch. The cube total never changes — it's always five.' Demo once with a child.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: Pause the game. Pick two volunteers who solved the same Hunt round in different ways. One used cubes-on-the-frame; one used fingers; one named instantly. Each child shows-and-tells their strategy in one sentence. Class votes on which felt fastest. Make the point: 'Different ways, same answer — but RECALL is fastest. Penny wants RECALL.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Two friends, two ways. Same five. Which way was fastest?' Affirm both, but flag instant-recall as the goal.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the Partners-of-5 tracker. Watch for children who can name the missing part instantly versus those who need to count.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Hide cubes yourself in front of the child: 'I have FOUR showing. How many are hiding?' Record their answer time on the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Allow these children to use a ten-frame mat with the 5 cells outlined. Place the visible cubes on the frame; the empty cells make the missing partner physically obvious.
differentiation.for_extending: Give the pair 7 cubes instead of 5 and have them hunt partners of 7. Stretches into A6.12 territory while staying on the same game mechanic.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Use the gesture 'hidden' (covered hand) and 'showing' (open hand) every time. Provide a visual cue card with the partner-equation pictures rather than words.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-CUBE PATH: Finger-only Partner Hunt. Two children sit knee-to-knee. Child A holds up some fingers (1-5); Child B names how many MORE to make 5 ('two fingers showing — THREE more to make 5'). Switch. No cubes, no ten-frames, no recording sheet — runs entirely on bodies. Whole lesson can run with NO purchased manipulatives, just hands and the anchor chart on the board.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child name the missing partner WITHOUT counting (instant recall = mastery)? Or do they count one-at-a-time (emerging)? Can they articulate that the total is always 5?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the tracker column for each child as you observe. The 'instant vs counting' column captures recall versus computation — important for A6.11 'recall' wording.

discussion_prompts: What was your favourite partner of 5? Why?
If 5 cubes are on the table and 4 are showing, how many are hiding? How do you know?
Why do we say plus and minus are friends?
Can you think of partners for a number that ISN'T 5? Maybe partners of 4, or partners of 3?
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. Then teacher holds up a hand showing some fingers. Children call out 'AND ___ to make 5.' (Three fingers up → 'and TWO to make 5.') Round the class once. Then each child takes their cube tower apart and pairs the colours into the take-home bag.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Partners-of-5 tracker for A6.11, plus the completed worksheet 'Partners of 5'. Observation note for which children connect plus and minus (the bridge to Lesson 3).
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: A6.11 says 'recall' — meaning the partner name should come out without recounting. The tracker's instant-vs-counting column is the key evidence. Children who still count are emerging; the lesson 3 story problems will catch their slow-recall and slow them down on situations to 10.

expanded_walkthrough.title: Partner Hunt — when the missing part is invisible (Carpenter & Moser CGI, 1983; Baroody, 2006; Resnick, 1983; Fuson, 1992)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A6.11 part-part-whole recall, the conceptual centre is the moment a child uses the partner relationship in the abstract — they can't see all five cubes, so they must USE the bond '3 and 2 make 5' as a FACT, not as a pile to recount.

Carpenter & Moser's (1983) Cognitively Guided Instruction (CGI) work classifies this as part-part-whole — the foundational schema that addition and subtraction share. K children move through three stages: build-from-cubes (concrete), counting-up (transitional), instant-recall (mastery). The Partner Hunt game is engineered to surface exactly this transition — visible cubes invite counting-up, but the goal is to build instant retrieval.

Resnick (1983) names commutativity (3+2 = 2+3) as the conceptual bridge that lets K children halve the number of facts they must memorise — five distinct partners of 5 instead of ten. The expected stretched response below explicitly checks for commutativity awareness.

Baroody (2006) traces single-digit addition development through three phases: counting-all (1+2 by counting 1, 2, 3), counting-on (1, then 2, 3), and direct retrieval (recall). K is the entry to phase 1; the Partner Hunt is the explicit attempt to push into phase 3 within 5.

Fuson (1992) shows that 'count-on' and 'count-up-to' are different cognitive moves — count-on (5+2: '5… 6, 7') and count-up-to (5−3: '3… 4, 5') — and that K children typically master the additive direction first. The 'Counts up' rescue in the recovery_moves below leans on Fuson's count-up-to construction.

The most common K trap is the child who can build any partner from cubes (Steps 1–2) but freezes when cubes are hidden (Step 4). The script below covers exactly what to say to that child.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pairs are at their tables. Each pair has 5 snap-cubes and one ten-frame mat. Player A is hiding some of their cubes under their hand; Player B is looking at the visible cubes and being asked to name the missing part. The teacher carries the formative tracker clipboard and stops at the pair where Player B is staring at the visible cubes without answering.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the pair. Player B is staring at three visible red cubes; Player A is hiding two yellow cubes under her hand. Player B has been silent for ~5 seconds. Don't say the answer. Instead, prompt the partner relationship.

'I see three cubes showing. How many cubes did your partner start with all together?' Wait. They'll usually say five (they helped count it before the hide). 'Five altogether. And how many are showing?' (Three.) 'So how many must be HIDING?'

If the child still doesn't see it, walk back to the cubes. 'Let's count up from three to five together. Three…' Hold up three fingers. 'Four…' Add one finger. 'Five.' Add another. 'How many fingers did I add?' (Two.) 'YES — two are hiding. Three and two make five — that's a partner.'

Now ask Player A to lift their hand and reveal. The child sees the two yellow cubes. 'Were you right?' Affirm. Repeat ONE more round with Player A hiding a different number. If the child names it instantly the second time, tick 'recall' on the tracker. If they still have to count up from the visible part, tick 'after counting' — that's still progress; recall comes with practice.

The long-term recovery move: send the child home with a 5-finger Partner Card. Each night's practice is one round of Partner Hunt with a parent. By the end of the week, the partners of 5 should be reflexive.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Stares at the visible cubes silently. The 'total of 5' fact has not yet been retrieved as memory; the cubes-in-hand model isn't yet abstract.
(Mid) Counts up from the visible number using fingers ('three… four… five — TWO!'). Has the relationship but uses counting, not recall.
(Strong) Names the missing partner instantly when shown the visible part: 'Two are hiding!' before the partner reveals their hand.
(Stretched) Volunteers extra information: 'Three and two make five, AND two and three make five — those are the SAME partner.' Has internalised commutativity.
common_misconceptions: The total can change when cubes are hidden. (Child believes the hide actually subtracts cubes from the world. Repair: count all five together BEFORE the hide so the child sees the total stays five.)

Each new partner is a fresh fact to memorise. (Child does not yet see 3+2 and 2+3 as the same partner. Repair: physically rotate the cube tower 180° so the colours swap positions; same five, same two parts.)

Partners of 5 only work with cubes. (Child hesitates when the same idea is asked with fingers, dots, or pennies. Repair: do the partner hunt three times with three different objects in the same week — cubes Day 2, fingers Day 3, pennies Day 5.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child believes the hide changes the total (says 'I don't know how many were there'): always count all 5 together BEFORE hiding any. The hide cannot change the total if the total was just established by class chorus. Repeat 3 rounds with the chorus-count BEFORE every hide.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child knows the total is 5 but can't yet retrieve the missing part (counts-all from 1): use Fuson's (1992) count-up-to rescue. Say 'how many more do we need to GET to 5?' rather than 'how many are missing?' Counting up from the visible 3 ('three… four, five — TWO more!') is a more accessible operation for K than 'subtract'. Encourage this verbally before any cube reveal.

DIAGNOSTIC C — child has the partner but doesn't see commutativity (treats 3+2 and 2+3 as separate facts to memorise — the Resnick 1983 trap): physically rotate the cube tower 180° so red and yellow swap positions; same five, same two parts. Pair every 3+2=5 written with 2+3=5, and every 5−3=2 with 5−2=3 — read aloud in 4-fact families ('plus, plus, minus, minus') to build the fact-family link explicitly.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of A6.11 — naming all six partners of 5 and connecting each addition fact to its related subtraction.

parts_outline.task: Six ten-frames printed across the page, each pre-filled with a different partner of 5 (e.g. 1 red + 4 yellow, 2 red + 3 yellow). The child writes the equation under each: __ + __ = 5.
Three Partner Hunt scenes: a tower of 5 with some cubes covered by Penny's hand. The child writes how many are hidden and the matching subtraction equation: 5 − __ = __.

Empty 'Partners of 5 anchor chart'. The child colours in two ten-frames and writes their own partner equation, then circles whether their partner is the SAME or DIFFERENT from a sibling partner already on the page.

expected_image_assets: Penny puppet thumbnail in the worksheet header
Six ten-frame visuals at letter scale (matching M4 manipulative)
Snap-cube illustrations in red and yellow
Quincy the piggy-bank cheering icon in a corner
